hero.title: Deliver Windows updates
hero.text: Give every Windows system one road for updates: SBD-WSUS01 on VLAN 20, fed across the air gap by WSUS’s export and import, delivering to four rings by Group Policy — with the domain controllers last, and by hand. Follow the build, explore the dependencies, and keep the evidence.

sample: HTTPS 8531 metadata · HTTP 8530 signed update files
Monthly, after Microsoft’s second-Tuesday release, beside SBD-REPO01’s snapshot
Rings 1–3 from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 (A02) · Ring 4 from AdminJumpBox01 (A01)

scene.label: Interactive 3D lesson network showing SBD-WSUS01 behind the core with both domain controllers and SBD-DHCP01, the 50 Windows PCs and both administration seats in front, and the update and console paths each lesson adds.
scene.completeCaption: Every Windows system takes updates only from SBD-WSUS01: a month’s content imported from hashed media, approved ring by ring, and installed on the domain controllers last, by Tier 0, one at a time.

nodes.name: SBD-WSUS01
nodes.title: SBD-WSUS01 · 10.0.20.30
nodes.description: The only road Windows updates travel. It never synchronizes: each month’s metadata and files arrive on hashed media and are imported. Members check metadata over HTTPS 8531 and pull signed files over HTTP 8530 (F06).

nodes.name: SBD-DC02
nodes.title: SBD-DC02 · 10.0.10.11
nodes.description: Ring 4. It downloads on its own but installs only when a Tier 0 operator starts it — the first of the two controllers, checked with dcdiag and repadmin before SBD-DC01 follows.

nodes.name: SBD-DC01
nodes.title: SBD-DC01 · 10.0.10.10
nodes.description: Ring 4, installed only after SBD-DC02 is healthy again. It is the PDC emulator and the domain’s time source, so it never restarts while its partner is down.

nodes.name: SBD-DHCP01
nodes.title: SBD-DHCP01 · 10.0.20.10
nodes.description: Ring 3, with the other member servers: it installs only what the pilot and the workstations have already proven, in its own install window.

nodes.name: 50 Windows PCs
nodes.title: 50 Windows PCs · 10.0.80.100–199
nodes.description: SBD-PC01–SBD-PC03 are Ring 1, the pilot; the other 47 are Ring 2. Each files itself into its ring by Group Policy and installs on its schedule, or at the approval’s deadline.

nodes.name: SBD-ADMIN-SRV01
nodes.title: SBD-ADMIN-SRV01 · 10.0.60.20
nodes.description: The Tier 1 seat (rule A02): the patch operators build and run SBD-WSUS01 from here, run each month’s import on it, and approve Rings 1 to 3. The seat itself sits in Ring 3.

nodes.name: AdminJumpBox01
nodes.title: AdminJumpBox01 · 10.0.60.10
nodes.description: The Tier 0 seat (rule A01): it owns the ring GPOs and the group changes, checks who approved each Ring 4 update, and installs the controllers by hand. It is the last system in Ring 4.

stepTitles: Write the Windows update rule and its exceptions
Place every Windows system in one of four rings
Put the domain controllers and Tier 0 last
Write the soak times and the stop rule
Set the monthly crossing beside SBD-REPO01’s
Confirm F06 and the console rows
design.mistake: Putting the domain controllers in the first ring because they matter most. A bad update would then reach the identity fabric first; Ring 4 goes last and installs only what three rings have already survived.
design.network: SBD-WSUS01 is planned on VLAN 20. The domain controllers, the member servers, the fleet and both administration seats run from earlier courses; no update path is shown until the server exists, and its content will only ever arrive on media.

control.name: Configuration Change Control
control.body: Rings make every update a controlled change: tried on the pilot, approved for the next ring only after it survives, and recorded at each step. Writing the order and the stop rule before the first update arrives makes the process reviewable.
control.question: Which systems could the network lose for a day without harm, and does your ring table put them first?

checklist: I wrote the Windows update rule with SBD-WSUS01 as its one source and SBD-ROOTCA01’s hand-carried exception.
I placed every Windows computer object in exactly one of the four rings and wrote down why it sits there, with SBD-AUDIT01 installed by its custodian.
I recorded the soak times, the stop rule and the monthly crossing beside SBD-REPO01’s, and confirmed F06, A01 and A02.

stepTitles: Build SBD-WSUS01 in the Servers OU
Install WSUS on WID and record its status
Configure a server that never synchronizes
Decide and record the update scope
Put metadata on TLS and keep files signed
Hold its administration to the tier model
wsus.mistake: Requiring TLS on the whole WSUS Administration site. Microsoft lists the five services that should require it; Content must not, and once it does, clients can no longer fetch update files over HTTP 8530 as rule F06 registers.
wsus.network: SBD-WSUS01 is live on VLAN 20 and administered from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01. It has no route out and no clients yet; its metadata port, 8531, now answers only over TLS with a certificate from the course 1.6 issuing CA.

control.name: Transmission Confidentiality and Integrity
control.body: Metadata — what to install, and the hash each file must match — travels over TLS on 8531, while the files stay on HTTP 8530 because each one is signed and checked against that hash. Integrity is protected end to end without encrypting every byte.
control.question: If someone could change the metadata in transit, what could they make a client do, and which setting stops them?

checklist: I installed WSUS on WID in the Servers OU, with files stored locally and synchronization manual and never run.
I recorded the scope — products, classifications and languages — and the decision to keep WID, with a review date.
I bound the SBD Server Authentication certificate to 8531, required TLS on the five services, and recorded the written Ring 4 procedure, its residual risk and the Tier 0 target.

stepTitles: Run the export server with the recorded scope
Download, export and copy the files
Hash and carry the set under custody
Compare, copy, then import on SBD-WSUS01
Check the import and file the crossing
wsus-offline.mistake: Importing first and comparing hashes afterwards — or not at all, because clients check signatures anyway. Microsoft warns never to import an export from a source you don’t trust; the hash comparison is how this network decides the media is still what left the connected side.
wsus-offline.network: No network path crosses the boundary: the month’s metadata package and update files arrive on approved media, carried by an authorized operator, and are imported on SBD-WSUS01 in a Tier 1 session from SBD-ADMIN-SRV01.

control.name: Software, Firmware, and Information Integrity
control.body: Every file is hashed on the connected side and again inside, and the import starts only when the two lists match. Microsoft’s signatures protect each update file a second time, when the client checks it.
control.question: Who could change the media between the two hash lists, and what in your custody record would show it?

checklist: I set the export server to exactly the products, classifications and languages recorded in lesson 2.
I compared the connected-side and lab-side hash lists with no differences before copying or importing anything.
I filed the crossing record with the carrier, dates, file count, package hash, both hash lists and the import log.

stepTitles: Create the ring groups and turn on client-side targeting
Build the ring GPOs around the same core
Set install behaviour and deadlines per ring
Link the GPOs and filter the pilot
Prove every computer reports to its ring
wsus-targeting.mistake: Linking one update GPO at the domain root for convenience. The domain controllers then take the workstations’ schedule and deadlines; each ring needs its own GPO, linked where its computers live, with Ring 4 installing only when Tier 0 starts it.
wsus-targeting.network: Every Windows system now checks SBD-WSUS01 for metadata over HTTPS 8531 and files itself into its ring: the PCs into Rings 1 and 2, the member servers into Ring 3, SBD-AUDIT01 into its own custodian-installed Ring 3 group, and the domain controllers into Ring 4. The ring GPOs come from AdminJumpBox01; nothing is approved yet.

control.name: Flaw Remediation
control.body: SI-2 asks that updates are tested before they are installed and installed within a set time. The rings do the first; the per-ring install times and deadlines do the second — except Ring 4, where a person starts each install deliberately.
control.question: What deadline would you set for Ring 2, and what would make you shorten it for an urgent fix?

checklist: I created the four ring groups and Ring 3 - Audit archive, switched WSUS to client-side targeting, and found Unassigned Computers empty.
I linked each ring’s GPO where its computers live and confirmed the pilot filter and link order with gpresult.
I read SBD-WSUS01 and the ring name in the policy values of one member of each ring, checking Ring 4 from AdminJumpBox01.

stepTitles: Approve the pilot, then promote on the soak times
Stop and roll back a failing update
Check Ring 4’s approvals, then install by hand
Report compliance and spot-check the systems
Clean up, then baseline SBD-WSUS01
Hand the records to course 1.15
wsus-prove.mistake: Approving the month’s updates for every group at once to save a week. The domain controllers then install something no ring has proven; approve for Ring 1 only, and promote once it has installed, reported and still works.
wsus-prove.network: The month’s approved updates flow ring by ring: the pilot first, then the workstations and member servers on their deadlines, SBD-AUDIT01 when its custodian installs, then the controllers by hand from AdminJumpBox01 — SBD-DC02, then SBD-DC01.

control.name: Flaw Remediation | Automated Flaw Remediation Status
control.body: WSUS’s per-ring reports show, without visiting a machine, which components still need an approved update — the automated status SI-2(2) asks for. Spot checks on the systems themselves keep that report honest.
control.question: How would you know if a computer stopped reporting altogether, rather than reporting itself compliant?

checklist: I promoted the month’s updates through Rings 1 to 3 on the written soak times recorded each promotion, and recorded the custodian’s install on SBD-AUDIT01.
I confirmed every Ring 4 approval names a Tier 0 account, and checked dcdiag and replication between the two controllers.
I filed the compliance reports, the spot checks, SBD-WSUS01’s first baseline with classified findings, and the hashed records.
